newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Sweden, Santer disagree over opt out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sweden, Santer disagree over opt out.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it would be up to European Union leaders to decide if Sweden could opt out of the single currency, despite Stockholm's insistence that it would act alone.
Jacques Santer, the Commission president, told a news conference that only EU heads of state and government could decide whether Sweden could skip monetary union if it qualified.
"It is up to the heads of state and government to take this decision," Santer said.
This would be based on polictical and economic factors, he said.

But Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, whose ruling Social Democratic Party executive decided on Tuesday that Sweden would not join economic and monetary union (EMU) at the launch, inisted his country would do what it wanted.
"Of course we have the right to remain outside," he told reporters in Stockholm.

The Maastricht treaty, which Sweden adopted when it became an EU member in 1995 only gives formal opt outs to Britain, which can decide to stay out, and Denmark, which has already said it will not take part.

The issue is sensitive because it involves an EU country deciding not to do something it has agreed to do on paper and Santer's comments seemed to reflect the Commission's role as the "guardian of the Treaty."
However, EU officials acknowledge privately that a country can not be forced to join EMU against its will, joking that the Commission would not send tanks onto the streets of Stockholm.
"It would be politically meaningless to force a country to join against its will," an EU source said. "The political reality is different from the legal reality."
Santer played down the Swedish move, saying it was only a statement by a political body.
"So far a government of a member state has not put in such an application...I don't concern myself with what happens within political parties or domestic politics," he said.
But he added that EMU would happen on time in 1999 regardless of Stockholm's attitude.
"I'm confident that we will maintain the deadline and we will have monetary union with or without Sweden," he said.
Persson, meanwhile, was firm in his position.
"I believe our statement is the political equivalent of an opt-out, although legally it may be something different," he said.
The decision was based on public and political EU scepticism at home and is widely expected to be confirmed by a party congress in September and later in the autumn by parliament.

The Dutch finance ministry earlier said Sweden did not have the right under the Maastricht Treaty to opt out. But it made clear that was only the opinion of the ministry, not of the Dutch EU presidency.
But the EU source said the problem need not arise if Sweden were judged not to meet the EMU entry criteria, noting that it is not a member of the bloc's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
"One could make the political and legal side compatible if one reaches the result that Sweden does not fulfil the requirements," the source said.
EU leaders are due to meet in late April or early May to decide which countries qualify for EMU.
